what_its_for: This vaccine helps protect you against a serious bacterial infection called meningococcal disease caused by Neisseria meningitidis type B (serogroup B). This infection can cause bacterial meningitis, which is a dangerous swelling of the brain and spinal cord lining, as well as a severe bloodstream infection. It is often given to teens, young adults, and people with certain medical conditions that raise their risk of this infection.
how_to_take: This vaccine is given as a shot (injection) into the muscle, usually in your upper arm. A trained healthcare provider, nurse, or pharmacist will give you this injection in a clinic, doctor's office, or pharmacy. You cannot give this vaccine to yourself at home. Stay in the waiting area for at least 15 minutes after getting the shot so staff can watch for any immediate reactions.
dosing: Most people receive 2 doses of this vaccine given at least 1 month (4 weeks) apart. Both doses are needed to get the best protection. Your doctor or pharmacist will tell you exactly when to come back for your second dose. People with certain immune system problems may need additional doses — your healthcare provider will guide you on the right schedule for your situation.
missed_dose: If you miss or forget to schedule your second dose, contact your doctor or pharmacist as soon as possible to reschedule. You do NOT need to restart the series from the beginning — just get the missed dose as soon as you can. Try to keep your vaccination appointments so you get full protection on time.
storage: This vaccine is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacist. It must be kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should never be frozen. You do not need to store this vaccine at home.
what_to_avoid: Tell your healthcare provider before getting this vaccine if you have ever had a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose of this vaccine or to any of its ingredients. Avoid getting this vaccine if you are currently very sick with a moderate or severe illness — it is usually better to wait until you feel better. There are no specific foods, drinks, or activities you need to avoid after getting this shot, but be gentle with the injection site arm for a day or two.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency medical care right away if you experience: difficulty breathing, swelling of your face, lips, throat, or tongue, a fast heartbeat, dizziness, or fainting shortly after the shot — these could be signs of a serious allergic reaction. Also contact your doctor if you develop a high fever (over 103°F / 39.4°C), severe redness or swelling at the injection site that gets worse after 24 hours, or if you feel very unwell in the days following vaccination. You should also report any unexpected side effects to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) at 1-800-822-7967.
when_it_works: Your body starts building protection after the first dose, but you are not fully protected until about 2 weeks after your second dose. It is important to complete both doses of the series to get the best immune response. Keep in mind that no vaccine is 100% effective, so continue to be aware of signs and symptoms of meningococcal disease even after vaccination.
special_populations: Teens and young adults (ages 16–23) are commonly vaccinated, with the preferred age being 16–18 years. People with a missing or non-functioning spleen, certain complement deficiencies, or those taking complement inhibitor medications (such as eculizumab) are at higher risk and should ask their doctor about vaccination. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals should discuss the risks and benefits with their healthcare provider before receiving this vaccine. Adults over 65 and young children under 10 years of age should consult their doctor, as dosing schedules and recommendations may differ. Always inform your provider of all your current medications, allergies, and health conditions before receiving any vaccine.
